summary: A periodic index memo from the RFC Editor summarizing the RFCs numbered 3200 through 3299. It is a catalog and not a protocol specification.

plainLanguage.summary: A librarian's list of one hundred new books with one line about each. This is that list for Internet documents.

subtitle: A catalog and brief summary of all RFCs numbered 3200 through 3299.

tldr.problem: Keeping track of newly published RFCs and understanding what they cover is difficult when standards and protocols proliferate rapidly across hundreds of specifications.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC Editor periodically publishes a summary document that lists every RFC in a given range with a one-paragraph description of its purpose and scope.
tldr.outcome: These periodic summaries serve as a finding aid and historical record of what standards were developed in a particular period. RFC 3299 covers the hundred RFCs published between 3200 and 3299 from 2001 to 2003.

today: RFC 3299 is an informational summary document from December 2003 that catalogs RFCs published in the early 2000s. It remains an Internet Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What This Document Is
sections.content:
RFC 3299 is a summary and index of RFCs numbered 3200 through 3299, covering one hundred specifications published between 2001 and 2003. It is an informational document, not itself a protocol specification. The RFC Editor publishes these summaries periodically to provide the Internet community with a catalog and overview of newly released RFCs.

Each entry includes the RFC number, author, publication date, a descriptive title, and a brief paragraph explaining the RFC's scope and purpose. Some RFCs are marked as being on the standards track, indicating they define protocols or procedures that may become Internet Standards.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a librarian's list of one hundred new documents, with one sentence about each to help you find what you need.

sections.title: Range and Coverage
sections.content:
The RFCs in this range span a wide variety of topics and categories. They include transport and application layer protocols, management information bases (MIBs) and management frameworks, security specifications, routing protocols, compression techniques, multimedia technologies, directory services, and administrative documents. Some are standards-track documents on their way to becoming Internet Standards or Draft Standards, while others are informational, experimental, or best-current-practice documents.

The 100-RFC range reflects the rapid growth of standardization work in the Internet community during this period. A single RFC number range might include everything from fundamental transport mechanisms to specialized application protocols to administrative guidance.
sections.plainLanguage: The hundred documents cover many different topics: how networks work, how to manage them, how to keep them secure, and many other things.

sections.title: Standards Track and Document Types
sections.content:
The document notes that many of the RFCs in the range are on the standards track, meaning they define specifications that can potentially become Internet Standards. However, because the status of RFCs can change during the standards development process, this summary only marks RFCs that are on the standards track at the time of publication. For the current and authoritative status of any RFC, the Internet Official Protocol Standards document should be consulted.

The RFCs covered include Proposed Standards (early-stage proposals), Draft Standards (more mature proposals being tested), Standards (fully adopted specifications), and Informational RFCs that provide useful information without seeking standardization.
sections.plainLanguage: Some documents become official standards after being tested. Others just provide helpful information. This list notes which documents are trying to become standards.

sections.title: Examples of RFCs in This Range
sections.content:
The RFCs numbered 3200 through 3299 include significant protocols and systems. RFC 3286 introduces SCTP, a new transport protocol for telecommunications. RFC 3293 and its related documents specify the General Switch Management Protocol (GSMP). RFC 3278 through 3281 define cryptographic algorithms and public key infrastructure. RFCs 3241 through 3243 address robust header compression for IP datagrams. RFC 3261 (not shown in this summary excerpt) defines the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP), a major signaling protocol for multimedia.

The range also includes many MIB specifications for network management, MIME type registrations, fax and messaging protocols, directory services, and infrastructure-related documents. This diversity reflects the breadth of topics covered by IETF standardization work.
sections.plainLanguage: In these hundred documents, you'll find new ways to send messages, manage networks, keep things secure, and many other innovations.

references.text: Ginoza, S., "Request for Comments Summary: RFC Numbers 3200-3299", RFC 3299, December 2003.
